source.title: HINT: Hierarchical Neuron Concept Explainer
source.authors: Andong Wang; Wei-Ning Lee; Xiaojuan Qi

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary file are present
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different neuron-to-concept measurement method to identify neurons associated with multiple concepts, and reports a bird/car example.
record.gate_note: HINT measures neuron contributions to hierarchical concepts. The clearest result for unrelated concepts is a VGG19 neuron associated with both bird and car. Results about localization performance, saliency-method evaluation, and adversarial or COVID-19 applications do not measure polysemanticity and are not rows.
record.test_reason: Different method (Shapley contributions to linear concept classifiers on VGG19 features.30) that flags neurons tied to several concepts. One example, neuron 199 (bird and car), bears on V1; the rest is method validation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that HINT builds low-cost neuron–hierarchical-concept associations and shows networks implicitly learn concept hierarchies. Identifying multimodal neurons, including bird/car, is a secondary demonstration, not a quantified finding.
record.recipe_differences: HINT uses saliency-guided feature-map regions, trained concept classifiers, and Shapley-value contribution scores; it is not the original neuron-interpretation method.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the measurement of multimodal neurons

fits_no_version.finding: In Inception v3 Mixed_6b (768 neurons), 711, 615 and 387 neurons have positive Shapley contributions to animal, person and plant. So many neurons contribute to several concepts under this score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under classifier-contribution scoring, most late-layer CNN neurons contribute to multiple high-level concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (venue as stated)
record.problems: The paper gives no numerical contribution values or uncertainty for the bird/car example in the text. It does not estimate the prevalence of multimodal neurons, and its example does not establish whether the two activations share a feature.
record.rows_left_out: Localization metrics, model comparisons, and other applications were left out because they evaluate HINT's localization or application performance rather than whether neurons respond to multiple unrelated concepts.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and the cat-face/car-front neuron; how common such neurons are; positive activation of one neuron to unrelated inputs measured directly.
All; no causal account of polysemanticity.
All; architectures are compared only for localization and contribution spread, not polysemantic share.
Whether bird/car share one feature is not analysed. Authors attribute the mammal/bird/reptile sharing to morphological similarity but do not test it.

missing.what: Same-level multimodal neurons for related concepts: 199 and 445 (mammal and bird); 322 and 347 (reptile and bird). Authors attribute these to shared morphology.
missing.locator: Section 4.2 'Concepts of the same level'; Figure 2(a); Figure S.4

missing.what: Neuron 445 is the top contributor to animal, vertebrate, mammal and carnivore (hierarchically nested concepts), shown in activation maps.
missing.locator: Section 4.2; Supp. E.2, E.3; Figures S.8–S.11, S.17–S.19

record.verdict_notes: Method paper; the polysemanticity evidence is a single qualitative example without numbers or uncertainty. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, cat faces, fronts of cars, or cat legs; it also does not estimate how common such mixtures are across neurons.
Language models, transformer MLP neurons, and token or context responses.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The share of polysemantic neurons as a function of activation, architecture, or regularization, and whether it can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons have one shared feature or related jobs, and whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare. The study does not analyze that question for its bird/car example.
Whether polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on ImageNet; training stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: HINT estimates neuron contributions to concepts using saliency-guided regions, concept classifiers, and Shapley values.
rows.measure: Neuron contribution to concepts; the paper reports that the neuron contributes to both bird and car. Numeric scores not stated in text.
rows.value: Contributes to both bird and car; the authors describe these concepts as conceptually far apart to humans.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Concepts of the same level; Supplementary Section E.3 and Figures S.20–S.21
rows.note: This is the study's explicit example of one neuron associated with two conceptually distant categories. The supplementary text describes activation maps on bird and car images; it says the neuron activates the bird's head while deactivating the car's wheels.
rows.check: The measure is the neuron's Shapley contribution to classifiers, not its response. Supp. E.3 says neuron 199 activates bird heads but deactivates car wheels. So it is not shown responding positively to both; no scores are given. The main text says the bird classifier detects bird body and car wheels, not that the neuron fires on both.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.2 'Concepts of the same level': 199th neuron contributes to both bird and car, concepts 'conceptually far part to humans'. Supp E.3 (Figs S.20, S.21): neuron 199 on VGG19 features.30 activates the bird's head and deactivates car wheels.
source_check.problem: No problem found. The neuron-199 E.3 text sits out of order in the extracted text, before the E.3 heading.

relationships.condition: VGG19 features.30, neuron 199, bird and car concepts, HINT contribution scores
relationships.reason: Neuron 199 contributes to both distant concepts (r1). But it activates on birds and deactivates on car wheels, so this is a signed classifier contribution, not a dual response.
relationships.display_finding: Neuron 199 contributed to both the bird and car concepts, which are semantically distant. However, it activated on birds and deactivated on car wheels, so this is a signed contribution to the classifier, not a response to both inputs.

relation.reason: Its own results (neuron 199's contributions and activation maps) bear on V1, though only through one qualitative example.

tranche.reason: A different method (saliency-guided regions, concept classifiers, Shapley contributions on VGG19 features.30) aimed at neurons tied to several concepts. It reports a bird/car neuron that bears on V1.

source_check.notes: Single qualitative example. The text states no numeric contribution values for neuron 199; the bar charts and Sankey figures (Figs S.4, S.8-S.16) hold them. The authors themselves call neuron 199 multimodal and say it 'can detect both bird and car'. The partial/limits_scope reading rests on its deactivation on car wheels (Supp E.3). The bird classifier also responds to car wheels (Fig 2 caption).

statements.correction: Neuron 199 (VGG19 features.30) pairs bird and car, and also mammal and bird. Neuron 445 pairs mammal and bird. Neurons 322 and 347 each pair reptile and bird. The authors attribute the mammal/reptile/bird pairings to shared morphological similarity, and call bird and car conceptually far apart.
statements.problem: Lists 199 among the study's 'other' same-level multimodal neurons, but 199 is the bird/car neuron itself, with a second pairing (mammal and bird). The rest is accurate: Shapley contributions, activates on bird head and deactivates on car wheels, no numeric values in the text.
Accurate for this study: Shapley contribution to concept classifiers; neuron 199 activates on bird heads and deactivates on car wheels (Supp E.3).
What it says about this study (one measure is a contribution, not a response) is accurate. Counts and other studies' claims were not checked here.
